title: Fourteen years
hook: Rama exiled; he accepts in one sentence

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaikeyi's two vara, old boons called in: Bharata crowned, Rama exiled. Words have weight. Now someone has to tell Rama, on the morning of his coronation.

Rama wakes up on his coronation morning. The city is decorated for him. The priests are ready. The water for the ceremony has been gathered from sacred rivers. A messenger comes: your father wants to see you. Rama walks into Kaikeyi's rooms expecting a blessing, and finds his father on the floor, unable to look at him, unable to speak. Kaikeyi speaks instead. Calmly, she tells him everything. Bharata will be king. You will go to the forest, dressed as a hermit, for fourteen years. Your father promised. Everyone in the room waits to see what Rama will do.
screen: `THE CORONATION MORNING.` → `HIS FATHER CAN'T SPEAK.` → `FOURTEEN YEARS IN THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Rama says, in effect: so be it. I'll go. He doesn't argue or bargain. He tells Kaikeyi he would have given the kingdom to Bharata gladly if anyone had simply asked. His only sorrow is that his father is in pain. Then he walks out. Valmiki notices one detail, and people have repeated it ever since: Rama's face didn't change. It looked the same when he heard he'd be king, and when he heard he'd be exiled. That isn't coldness. The people around him are anything but calm. His mother Kausalya is devastated. His brother Lakshmana is furious and ready to fight their father for the throne. Rama is the steady one, and he talks Lakshmana down. Why does he accept? Dharma, your third word: doing what's yours to do. For Rama, keeping his father's word is his duty, even when it costs him everything. That's why tradition calls him maryada purushottam: the ideal person, who keeps within the bounds of right action. Not everyone finds this easy. Some readers ask whether Rama should have fought, and the tradition lets them ask. But the scene draws a line worth keeping: giving up and accepting are different. Giving up sits down. Accepting stands up and starts walking. Rama doesn't pretend it's fair; he just refuses to let the unfairness decide who he is. The Gita's line is hiding here too: the action is yours, the fruit isn't. Accept, then walk.
screen: `SO BE IT. I'LL GO.` · `HIS FACE DIDN'T CHANGE.` · `DHARMA: KEEP THE FATHER'S WORD.` · `ACCEPTING ISN'T GIVING UP.` · then, large: `ACCEPT, THEN WALK.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that isn't fair and won't change: a diagnosis, a loss, a decision someone else made. Don't argue with it for now; let your face be still, the way Rama's was. Breathe in: this is what is. Breathe out: what's my next step?
Fourteen years. Rama's exile, accepted in a sentence, on the morning he was meant to be crowned.
Your line: accept, then walk. Even fourteen years begin with one step. That's forty days in.

howItsDone: Many Hindus hold up Rama's acceptance of exile as the model of keeping one's word and duty; the scene is often retold when families talk about hard decisions and honoring parents.

what it means: Rama chooses to keep his father's word, and his calm isn't coldness but a refusal to let unfairness decide who he is.
what a scholar hears: maryada purushottam, the ideal man within the bounds of dharma, is a later devotional title; Valmiki's detail of the unchanged face is the seed of it.

chat.says: When Rama agreed to go into exile, wasn't he just giving up?
options: No. He accepted it, then started walking. Giving up sits down.
Yes. He was too upset to argue, so he quietly gave in.
No. He planned to fight his father once he'd left the city.
chat.meaning: Rama keeps his father's word as his dharma. Accepting isn't giving up: it stands up and starts walking.
